title: Packages, Bumps and Quotas: Products, Pricing and Entitlements
basis: Reconstructed on 2026-11-12 from the published index.md (paragraph for paragraph, in its own order) and spec.md (accepted 2026-10-21), which it replaces. Intent outcome, acceptance criteria AC-1 to AC-3, the thesis and the role are copied unchanged from the products-and-entitlements entry in journal-spec.json. Units added to the published text: the roadmap paragraph p04, the trade-offs paragraph p43 and the synthesis paragraph p59.

know: Product catalog, pricing engine, entitlement, quota and effect, and why catalog, price, entitlement and bill stay separate.

The entitlement ledger's entry types with idempotency keys, effect projection onto the listing document as explicit paid fields, enforcement points with fail-open and fail-closed behavior, and quotas meeting feeds.
Metering, billing, revenue recognition over the display period, credit notes, and the sold-versus-delivered reconciliation.
believe: An entitlement is a ledger, not a counter, and a price event should be a data release, not a code release.
Every invoice line must trace to delivery evidence, which serves revenue assurance, dispute answers and paid-ranking disclosure from one pipeline.
can_do: Replace scattered package checks with four separated concerns joined by events.
Specify an entitlement matrix: product, enforcement point, effect, delivery evidence and owner.
Plan a migration onto a shared entitlement service with shadow billing months and a reconciliation rule for cutover.

audience.who: Principal engineers and architects who own monetization, search or billing integration at a marketplace or a marketplace group, and engineering leaders deciding whether to build or buy billing and entitlements.
already_knows: APIs, databases, event streams, search engines and Kubernetes (the book's baseline); idempotency and append-only event logs.

From earlier chapters: the ten monetization models, VAS (value-added services), packages, the package staircase and Autotrader's annual price event (monetization-models); the listing event contract and the event backbone; ranking's paid boosts and its relevance floor; the feed contract and Motorvane's DMS feeds (listing-ingestion); seller accounts and Agence Rhône Habitat's branches (sellers-and-accounts); Omnibus, P2B and the DSA (marketplace-regulation).

Veldmark (fictional), its brands Tradeyard, Motorvane, Hearthly and Keybridge, Common Ground, the architecture advice forum, Yardstick, the cast (Ingrid Halvorsen, Olivier Petit, Felix Brandt, Yara Mendes), Autohaus Ruhrblick and the Essen Golf, and the failure-pattern names (Billing by Guesswork, Multiplier Creep, Deal-Shaped Architecture, Ghost Inventory, Search as System of Record).
does_not_know: The terms this chapter owns: product catalog, pricing engine, entitlement, quota, effect, delivery evidence, effect projector and enforcement point.
Billing and finance terms: overage, proration, dunning, credit notes, revenue recognition over the display period, variable consideration, CPQ (configure-price-quote).
How packages, quotas, feeds and price events interact in practice.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given an overbilling dispute and a slow price event, the reader names the shared cause and the design that removes it.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A dealer on a 150-slot package is billed overage for 13 cars that were never published: the feed importer enforced the quota and skipped them, while a monthly billing export counted the feed file. Separately, a group price change across four brands is estimated in engineering weeks. Using only this chapter: what is the common cause, and what do you build?
acceptance_criteria.expected: There is no single record of what can be sold, what a seller holds and what was delivered. Keep catalog, pricing engine, entitlement ledger and billing apart; record grants, consumptions and refused publications as append-only entries with idempotency keys, so billing reads 150 consumptions and no overage; project effects onto the listing read model as explicit paid fields; emit delivery events and reconcile them daily with grants and invoice lines; hold products and prices as versioned catalog data so a price event is a reviewed data release.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the opening alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first heading) can predict the chapter's sections.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the callouts and the paragraphs before the first heading: what will this chapter discuss, in what order, and with what kind of evidence?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The commercial core every monetization model needs and Part VI's test that what was sold was delivered; the four terms the chapter owns; that the design is a reference-architecture inference anchored to published product behavior; then the Ruhrblick overbilling, the four concerns, the commercial core's architecture (ledger, effects, enforcement points, quotas and feeds, metering and billing, sold versus delivered), the public record, the Veldmark worked example with Tally, trade-offs, vertical differences, failure modes, the Chief Architect's view and questions. Evidence: dated investor sources (Rightmove, Autotrader, CarGurus, OLX, Vinted, Adevinta), Stripe documentation, EU law and the fictional Veldmark.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reverse outline of the chapter, written without the spec, lists the same controlling ideas in the same order as the post spec's sections and paragraphs.
Given a proposal that ranking ask the entitlement service per candidate, the reader says why not, where paid effects live instead and what must remove them.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Your search team proposes that the ranking stage call the entitlement service for every candidate to check whether it holds a paid top position, so the answer is always current. Using only this chapter: why should you refuse, where should paid state live instead, and what must happen when a listing with a paid top position is sold?
acceptance_criteria.expected: At a peak of 31,000 queries a second with about 400 candidates per query, live lookups mean on the order of 12 million entitlement answers a second, which no ledger should serve. An effect projector consumes ledger events and writes explicit paid fields (such as paid.top_eligible_until, paid.label, paid.product_version) onto the listing document in the search index, so ranking reads them with the listing; effects may be a little stale, the ledger may not; the index is never the record and is re-projected from the ledger on a rebuild. The projector also consumes listing lifecycle events, and a sold, removed or blocked listing carries no paid fields, whatever days remain, or it becomes Ghost Inventory with a price tag.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given an outage of the entitlement service and a dealer feed above its package, the reader states what each enforcement point does and where that policy is recorded.
acceptance_criteria.probe: The entitlement service is down for an hour on a weekday. During it, a private seller tries to buy a paid publication, a dealer's feed arrives with 163 cars for a 150-slot package, and buyers keep searching. Using only this chapter: what should insertion, feed import and ranking each do, and where is the rule for the dealer's 13 extra cars written down?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Paid consumer publication fails closed until payment is confirmed (free listings fail open); feed import queues and retries, never skipping silently, and reports to the feed; ranking serves the last projected effects and logs them as stale. Failing open is the default for what a paying professional already holds, documented per enforcement point, because failing closed protects revenue but damages supply. The overflow policy (reject excess, dealer priority, publish all and bill overage, or publish and prompt to upgrade) is a term of the contract stored with the entitlement, not importer behavior; each refused car gets a PublishRefused entry and appears in the feed report, and billing counts published listings from the ledger, not feed rows.

thesis.question: How do you architect what a seller can buy, what they are entitled to, and how they are billed?
thesis.claim: The commercial core behind paid products should keep four concerns apart, a versioned product catalog, a pricing engine, an entitlement ledger and billing, so that a price event is a reviewed data release rather than a code release; entitlements should be an append-only ledger of grants, consumptions, releases, expiries and refunds with idempotency keys rather than counters in each service; enforcement points should read effects projected through events as explicit paid fields on the listing read model, never asking the ledger live and never letting an effect outlive the listing's sale or removal; and insertion, ranking, rendering and lead routing should emit delivery events that a daily reconciliation compares with grants and invoice lines, so that every invoice line traces to delivery.
thesis.disputed_by: The common practice of writing package checks as conditions in the insertion service, the search query and the card template, with a monthly billing export counting by its own definition; or a counter service per quota; or a billing vendor's feature switches taken as the entitlement system.
thesis.so_what: A Chief Architect who accepts this makes the catalog model, the entitlement ledger, the effect schema and the delivery-evidence events group standards while leaving products, prices and contract terms to brands, writes an entitlement matrix naming each product's enforcement point, effect, evidence and owner, buys invoicing, tax and collection but builds the catalog, ledger and effect projector, moves each brand only after a shadow billing month reconciles with no unexplained difference, and watches the daily unexplained difference in euros.
thesis.how_why: Motorvane counted a dealer's cars twice: the feed importer published 150 of Autohaus Ruhrblick's 163 cars and skipped 13, while the billing export counted the feed file and charged €117 overage for cars never live; an audit found 1,140 dealers overbilled by about €212,000 over 14 months. The same missing record made the 1 January 2028 price event an estimate in engineering weeks per brand. At Veldmark's Sunday peak of 31,000 queries a second, a ranking stage asking the ledger live for 400 candidates per query (an illustrative figure) would need on the order of 12 million answers a second, so effects must ride on the listing document. Under Tally, Ruhrblick's month records 150 consumptions and 13 refused publications, and the invoice carries no overage line.

supporting_claims.claim: Billing by Guesswork is structural: when the commercial fact of what a seller holds is counted separately by enforcement and billing and products live in each brand's code, the marketplace overbills sellers and turns every price event into engineering work, both for lack of one record of what was sold, held and delivered.

Catalog, pricing engine, entitlement ledger and billing stay apart, with products as versioned catalog data that grant explicit effects and prices as effective-dated price lists whose quotes record every input version, so that a price event is a reviewed data release.

Entitlements are an append-only ledger shared by the consumer and professional selling paths, with grants, consumptions, releases, expiries, suspensions and refunds as entries carrying idempotency keys from the business event, which makes every balance explainable and every invoice reconcilable.

Enforcement points read effects projected by events as explicit paid fields on the listing read model, never the ledger live; effects never outlive the listing's sale or removal, failure behavior is decided per enforcement point, and quota policy for feeds is a contract term recorded in the ledger.

Billing consumes the ledger and metering rather than recounting, and a daily reconciliation of grants, delivery evidence and invoice lines makes every invoice line traceable, which serves revenue assurance, seller reports, dispute answers and paid-ranking disclosure from one pipeline.

A group makes the catalog model, the ledger, the effect schema and the delivery-evidence events shared standards while brands keep products, prices and terms, buys invoicing, tax and collection but builds the catalog, ledger and projector, and migrates each brand only after a shadow billing month reconciles.

role.contribution: Designs the commercial core that implements every monetization model and supplies the part's proof that what was sold was delivered, with paid effects that ranking and advertising consume.

additional_patterns.applies_to: the scene poses the Ruhrblick invoice and the price-event estimate as one problem; the worked example replays both under Tally after the body has built the design

the architecture section follows a paid product's life: sold through one of two paths, recorded in the ledger, projected as effects, read at enforcement points (including feed import), metered and billed, and reconciled against delivery

flow.rationale: The scene comes first because the chapter's design is the answer to its two problems. The concepts come next because every later section uses catalog, price, entitlement, quota, effect and delivery evidence. The architecture follows a paid product from sale to reconciliation; effects cannot be explained before the ledger they are projected from, and reconciliation needs the delivery evidence that the concepts define as emitted by the systems that deliver value, which the reconciliation paragraph names (insertion, ranking, rendering, lead routing). The public record comes after the design, so the reader can see what each documented behavior requires of it, and before the worked example, whose build-or-buy decisions rest on it. The worked example can replay the invoice and the price event only once the whole core exists. Trade-offs, vertical differences, failure modes, the Chief Architect's view and the questions apply the whole design, so they come last; placed earlier, they would weigh options the reader has not yet seen.

sections.heading: Setting the Scene at Veldmark: Thirteen Cars and €117
sections.controlling_idea: A €117 overage for thirteen unpublished cars and a price event estimated in engineering weeks are one problem: Veldmark has no single place that says what can be sold, what a seller holds and what was delivered.

advances_thesis.how: Shows Billing by Guesswork as a structural defect with a cost in credits and in delivery speed.

flow.rationale: The disputed invoice comes first because it is concrete; its structural cause follows, then the second agenda item, so that Ingrid's framing can join them. Putting the price event first would make the invoice look like a separate bug.

transition_in.carries_over: The wrong of billing a dealer for cars the platform refused to publish.
transition_in.introduces: Autohaus Ruhrblick's August invoice.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: In late September 2027 Autohaus Ruhrblick disputes €117 of overage on its August Motorvane invoice for 13 cars that were never published.

evidence.what: Pro 150: 150 slots for €1,450 a month, €9 per car per month overage; the DMS feed delivered 163 cars; 150 were live; 13 billed at €117.
evidence.shows: Gives the dispute in figures a reader can check.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The overbilling is structural: the feed importer skipped cars above the quota while the billing export counted the feed file, so two correct counters billed 1,140 dealers about €212,000 over 14 months.

evidence.what: Felix Brandt's trace; the audit of 14 months: 1,140 dealers, about €212,000, all credited in October 2027.
evidence.shows: Shows the defect is the design, not one dealer's bad luck.

evidence.what: Figure 1: a feed of 163 cars, a quota gate that publishes 150 and skips 13, and a separate counter that bills all 163.
evidence.shows: Pictures the two counters.

transition_in.introduces: Its cause: two counters for one fact.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Olivier's group-wide price-and-product event on 1 January 2028 is estimated in engineering weeks because each brand's products and packages are hard-coded in its own stack.

evidence.what: Tradeyard VAS hard-coded in Yardstick (PHP); Motorvane packages in a Kotlin service and the sales CRM; Hearthly tiers in a Go contract service; Keybridge billing on its own .NET stack.
evidence.shows: Shows why a price change is a code change at every brand.

transition_in.carries_over: The Ruhrblick case at the architecture advice forum.
transition_in.introduces: A second agenda item: the price event.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Ingrid frames both items as one problem, the lack of a single place that says what can be sold, what a seller holds and what was delivered, which Common Ground's catalog and entitlement goal for Q2 2028 must answer.

evidence.what: Common Ground's goal of one product catalog and entitlement service by Q2 2028.
evidence.shows: Sets the target the chapter's design meets.

transition_in.carries_over: The invoice and the price-event estimate.

sections.heading: Concepts: Four Things That Must Stay Apart
sections.controlling_idea: The single place Veldmark lacks is four concerns kept apart, catalog, pricing engine, entitlement ledger and billing, joined by delivery evidence, with effects as what enforcement points read.

advances_thesis.how: Defines the separation and the vocabulary the architecture uses.

flow.rationale: The four concerns and delivery evidence come first as the whole; each of the first three concerns is then defined in turn, catalog before price because a price is the price of a catalog item, and entitlement last because it is bought at a price and grants a catalog effect. Defining entitlements before the catalog would leave 'effect' undefined.

transition_in.introduces: The four concerns that, kept apart, form that place.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The chapter's core decision is to keep four concerns apart, each answering one question, changing for its own reasons, with its own owner and things it must not contain.

evidence.what: Product catalog, pricing engine, entitlement ledger, billing: question answered, when it changes, owner, must not contain.
evidence.shows: Shows that each concern changes for different reasons and has a different owner, which is why merging them fails.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Delivery evidence, the record of what the platform actually did, is an input the four concerns share but none owns: delivery systems emit it, and the ledger, billing and reporting consume it.

evidence.what: Listings published under a slot, impressions in a paid position, boosts executed, leads routed.
evidence.shows: Makes delivery evidence concrete.

transition_in.introduces: The one input the four share but none owns.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The subsections define the first three concerns; billing is a finance system the chapter connects to rather than designs, and its interface comes under Architecture.

transition_in.carries_over: The four concerns and delivery evidence.
transition_in.introduces: Which concerns the following subsections define and where billing is handled.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A catalog has five object types, product, package, add-on, effect (what an item does at an enforcement point) and product version, and the effect is the one most catalogs forget.

evidence.what: Bump, Top listing (7 days), Highlight; Pro 150 = 150 slots + 20 boosts + statistics + Co-Driver-style tooling.
evidence.shows: Shows products and packages in the book's terms.

evidence.what: Rightmove: 'more than 50% of independent agents purchased incremental product above their package commitment'.
evidence.shows: Shows add-ons in a published result.

evidence.what: Without versions, changing a product silently changes what past buyers bought.
evidence.shows: Shows why product versions are part of the catalog.

transition_in.carries_over: The catalog named as the first concern.
transition_in.introduces: Its five object types.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The catalog is reference data shipped as releases: versioned, reviewed, effective-dated and published as events that downstream services cache.

evidence.what: The same treatment as the category taxonomy in categories-and-taxonomies.
evidence.shows: Ties the rule to a pattern the reader already knows.

transition_in.introduces: How the catalog is released.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A price is a function, not a field: a marketplace price depends on at least ten dimensions, from country and category to contract, date and experiment arm.

evidence.what: Ten pricing dimensions with an example and why each matters.
evidence.shows: Shows how many inputs a single price has, which is why prices cannot be a field on a product.

transition_in.carries_over: The catalog: what can be sold.
transition_in.introduces: The pricing engine: what it costs.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Vinted's public price list shows formula pricing in practice, with the buyer fee and the bump fee varying by order and item characteristics.

evidence.what: Buyer fee varies by 'item characteristics, order value, order type'; bump fee by duration, item price and 'territorial scope (local or international)'.
evidence.shows: Shows a real marketplace pricing by formula.

transition_in.introduces: A documented example.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Two design rules follow: prices are effective-dated, reversible price-list versions, and every price quote records the version of every input that produced it.

evidence.what: Autotrader's 'annual 1 April 2025 pricing and product event'.
evidence.shows: Shows the kind of event effective-dated price lists exist for.

evidence.what: A quote with catalog, price-list, contract, promotion and experiment versions can be reproduced exactly in a dispute six months later.
evidence.shows: Shows why quotes carry versions.

advances_thesis.how: Makes a price event a data release.

transition_in.carries_over: Prices as functions of many dated inputs.
transition_in.introduces: The two rules that follow.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: An entitlement has a holder, a product version, a validity window, an optional quantity and a source; a quota is an entitlement that consumption reduces, and at run time an effect is the projection of active entitlements an enforcement point needs.

evidence.what: 'account 88412 may hold 150 active vehicle listings and currently holds 150'; 'listing 5531 is top-eligible in category city bikes, Rotterdam, until 14 March 23:59'.
evidence.shows: Shows effects as the answers an enforcement point needs.

transition_in.introduces: The third concern: entitlements, quotas and effects.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Separating entitlement from effect keeps the hot paths fast, because enforcement points need only the effect and only the entitlement service reads entitlements.

evidence.what: Ranking needs a boolean, a category, a window and a cap, not whether a top position came from a promotion or a contract.
evidence.shows: Shows how little the hot path needs.

advances_thesis.how: Sets up effect projection.

transition_in.carries_over: Effects defined as projections of entitlements.
transition_in.introduces: Why the separation matters on hot paths.

sections.heading: Architecture: The Commercial Core
sections.controlling_idea: The commercial core follows a paid product from two selling paths through an append-only ledger and projected effects to enforcement points, metering and billing, and a daily reconciliation of sold against delivered.

advances_thesis.how: Builds the ledger, the projection and the reconciliation the thesis claims.

flow.rationale: The section follows a paid product's life: how it is sold, where the sale is recorded, how the record reaches the hot paths, how those paths enforce it and how feeds meet quotas, how it is billed, and how delivery is checked against the bill. Effects before the ledger would project from nothing; reconciliation before enforcement would compare evidence from points the reader has not met. The billing rule (p33) sits next to the billing definition (p31) so the finance requirements do not split mechanism and rule.

transition_in.carries_over: The four concerns and delivery evidence, defined.
transition_in.introduces: How they connect as one core, starting where money comes in.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The commercial core starts with two selling paths that share almost nothing operationally: prepaid consumer purchases and postpaid professional contracts.

evidence.what: Figure 2: the commercial core as five stages, define, sell, hold, deliver, settle, with delivery evidence flowing back; the prose maps the four concerns onto the stages.
evidence.shows: Gives the whole core before its parts.

evidence.what: A €3.99 bump bought on a phone; Pro 150 for 24 months at a 6% discount with overage.
evidence.shows: Contrasts the two paths.

evidence.what: Vinted: a bump bought while a listing is in review is not processed or charged.
evidence.shows: Shows a rule the consumer path must encode.

evidence.what: CarGurus packages on 'monthly, quarterly, semiannual, or annual' terms that 'generally auto-renew on a monthly basis and are cancellable by dealers with 30 days'' notice.
evidence.shows: Shows the shape of professional contracts.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The two paths should share the catalog, the pricing engine and the entitlement ledger and nothing else, so a bump bought by a private seller and one in a dealer package are the same product version in the same ledger.

evidence.what: Payment and order-to-cash paths differ in regulation, tooling and failure modes; one billing system forced on both usually serves neither.
evidence.shows: Shows why only the three concerns are shared.

transition_in.introduces: What they must have in common.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The ledger is append-only: every change is an entry with a type, a creator and an idempotency key, never an update of a counter.

evidence.what: Grant, Consume, Release, Expire, Suspend/Resume, Revoke/Refund, Adjust: created by, example, idempotency key.
evidence.shows: Shows that every business event that changes what a seller holds has its own entry and key.

evidence.what: Figure 3: the ledger as a ticket book with a journal.
evidence.shows: Pictures balances as sums of entries.

transition_in.introduces: Its entry types.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Because the balance is the sum of entries, the ledger gains three properties: idempotency, explainability and reconciliation.

evidence.what: Stripe: an idempotency key lets a client 'safely repeat the request without risk of creating a second object or performing the update twice'.
evidence.shows: Grounds idempotency in a documented principle.

evidence.what: The Ruhrblick invoice would have been computed from Consume and PublishRefused entries.
evidence.shows: Shows reconciliation on the chapter's case.

evidence.what: Figure 4: the lifecycle of an entitlement, every transition a ledger entry.
evidence.shows: Shows Suspended and Revoked as the transitions most often forgotten.

advances_thesis.how: Shows what the ledger makes possible.

transition_in.introduces: The three properties that follow.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Enforcement points need answers in milliseconds, so effects are projected onto the read models the hot paths already use: at Veldmark's Sunday peak, live lookups would mean more than 12 million entitlement answers a second.

evidence.what: 31,000 queries per second at the Sunday peak; 400 candidates per query is an illustrative figure; more than 12 million answers per second.
evidence.shows: Shows why the ledger cannot be asked live.

advances_thesis.how: Shows why effects must ride on the listing document.

transition_in.introduces: Why hot paths cannot read it directly.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The effect projector consumes ledger events, publishes effect-change events on the backbone, and writes per-listing effects as explicit paid fields on the listing document.

evidence.what: ListingPaidEffectChanged and AccountQuotaChanged on the group event backbone.
evidence.shows: Names the events in Veldmark's design.

evidence.what: paid.top_eligible_until, paid.top_scope, paid.bump_time, paid.highlight, paid.label, paid.product_version: example and user.
evidence.shows: Shows that each paid effect is a separate, explicit field with a named consumer.

transition_in.introduces: The projector and the fields it writes.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Ranking owns how the paid fields are used, under its standard that relevance models never read them; this chapter owns producing them correctly and removing them promptly.

evidence.what: Ranking's group standard: no paid fields as features, a relevance floor for reserved slots, every paid impression logged.
evidence.shows: Draws the boundary with ranking.

transition_in.introduces: Who uses them and who produces them.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A paid effect that outlives its listing is Ghost Inventory with a price tag, so the projector must consume listing lifecycle events and sold, removed or blocked listings carry no paid fields.

evidence.what: A sold bike keeps its top slot because ListingSold reached search but not the projector.
evidence.shows: Shows the failure a buyer would see.

transition_in.introduces: What happens when removal fails, and the rule that prevents it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Two consistency rules apply to every effect: effects tolerate bounded staleness while the ledger does not, and the index is never the record.

evidence.what: A top-listing effect 20 seconds after payment is acceptable; a slot granted twice is not; after an index rebuild effects are re-projected from the ledger.
evidence.shows: Shows each rule at work and how it avoids Search as System of Record.

transition_in.introduces: Two more rules for every effect.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Each enforcement point reads effects within its own latency budget, and its behavior when the ledger is unavailable is a commercial decision: fail open on what a paying professional holds, fail closed only on new consumer charges, documented per point.

evidence.what: Seven enforcement points (insertion, feed import, ranking, rendering, lead routing, pro tools, scheduler): question, reads, latency budget, behavior on ledger unavailability.
evidence.shows: Shows that each point has a different budget and a different safe failure.

evidence.what: Failing closed protects revenue and damages supply; failing open protects supply and costs revenue that reconciliation can recover.

conclusion.heading: From Products to Attention
conclusion.synthesis: Ruhrblick's €117 and the price-event estimate had one cause, and one record answers both: the ledger that shows 150 consumptions and 13 refused publications is the ledger a price-list release writes to, the source of the paid fields ranking reads, and the evidence finance signs and a disclosure rests on.
conclusion.so_what: A group that builds this record once can change prices as data, sell across brands and prove every invoice line; one that leaves package checks scattered pays for each brand's counting and learns of its errors from its dealers.

callback.to: The scene: Ruhrblick's €117 overage and the price event estimated in engineering weeks, and the opening's wronged seller.
callback.how: The reader now sees both as the same missing record, closed by the ledger, the projection and the reconciliation.

takeaway.content: Build one ledger of what was sold, held and delivered before the next price event, and bill only from it.

hand_off.carries_over: The commercial core turns monetization models into things that can be sold, held, enforced, delivered and billed, but one family of paid products still needs its own machinery.
hand_off.introduces: Advertising, which sells the audience rather than the listing, to brands and agencies rather than sellers, through ad servers, header bidding and consent signals.

evidence.shows: Calls back to the scene and shows both problems closed by the same record.
